Tesla’s $30,000 Cybercab comes with a $299 monthly catch

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (919 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Or in the case of Tesla’s self-driving Cybercab, several.
  • Recent findings suggest that last Friday night, Tesla said it had invited “select customers” to purchase their very own Cybercabs.
  • From there, though, the Cybercab will need constant cash infusions to stay on the road.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There is always a catch. Or in the case of Tesla’s self-driving Cybercab, several.

Recent findings suggest that last Friday night, Tesla said it had invited “select customers” to purchase their very own Cybercabs. The two-seat, gold vehicle is unlike any other on the market: It lacks a steering wheel and brake pedals, and is primarily driven by software. (Other autonomous vehicle companies, including Alphabet’s Waymo and Amazon’s Zoox, offer self-driving rides on ride-hail networks, but don’t let people buy their cars.) Tesla’s “limited release” will supposedly offer some people (unclear how many) the opportunity to pay $29,900 to take delivery in December.

From there, though, the Cybercab will need constant cash infusions to stay on the road.

The business model raises questions about what people will actually get when they buy a Cybercab. “You’ll never really own the car,” states Ivan Drury, the director of insights at Edmunds. “It’s more like $30,000 to buy into a franchise.”.

According to recent reports, according to documents posted on Tesla’s website, the vehicle “will not operate” without what Tesla is calling an “autonomy subscription,” a monthly fee that will start at $299. If owners don’t pay on time and in full, their self-driving cars won’t work. If they try to operate the vehicles in areas that don’t support the service—right now, they’re restricted to portions of cities in Florida and Texas—their self-driving cars won’t work. (That area can expand, contract, or “relocate” at any time.).

In a recent development, if owners do anything that Tesla deems “unauthorized or inappropriate,” the firm indicates it can suspend or cancel the subscription—and their self-driving cars won’t work. If the vehicle loses connectivity, the self-driving cars won’t work. (“Tesla is not responsible for carrier, spectrum, environmental, or other external outages,” its “autonomy agreement” says.).

Tesla also reserves the right to make an owner’s car not work at any time: It claims it can, for any safety or security purpose, suspend or terminate access to Cybercab tech, or restrict operations by location, road type, weather, or “condition.” This is particularly salient because the Cybercab is also under investigation by US safety regulators, who are trying to understand why Tesla believes the vehicle meets safety standards without so many of the parts and systems required.

Tesla didn’t respond to a request for comment.

For years, automakers have seen increasingly software-dominated vehicles as an opportunity to get drivers hooked on the same special sauce that makes Netflix, Amazon, and Spotify so potent: monthly subscription services. Because these vehicles can receive over-the-air software updates, manufacturers can offer drivers fresh services as they make them. The upside is high, tech-style margins that keep rolling in, versus the razor-thin ones seen in car-making. A 2024 report suggested that connected-car features could one day be a $200 billion industry.

In some ways, the subscription model is working. Today, some automakers charge extra for remote start, security, Internet connectivity, and advanced driver assistance features. General Motors noted it made $2.7 billion in subscription-related revenue last year from fees drivers paid for its OnStar and Super Cruise services.

Sources indicate that but some customers have also found the business model yucky, or even offensive. Why charge extra to “unlock” a feature that’s already built into a car? If an automaker can add a new feature at any time, can’t they also take it away? And if they can take it away, what does “ownership” mean? In 2022, BMW told drivers in select countries it would activate factory-installed heated seats for a monthly or one-time fee; it eventually backed down after public outcry, pledging the company would no longer charge subscription fees for preinstalled hardware. (BMW is still pursuing a subscription model for some features.) “Consumers hate being nickel-and-dimed for subscriptions,” states Drury.

Sources indicate that tesla was an early mover in the subscription feature space and has offered connectivity and driver-assistance features for monthly or one-time fees for a decade. As the company has shifted away from making cars and toward robotics and autonomous vehicles, executives have made clear that charging for services is the future. (Its Robotaxi service currently picks up fare-paying passengers in parts of eight US cities.) So Tesla buyers may be particularly amenable to paying monthly to make their self-driving cars go.

In exchange for monthly fees, buyers will also get access to other services, too, including remote support, roadside assistance, tire, air filter, and windshield wiper replacements, and tire and camera inspections. (The agreement says that list might change, too.) Cybercabs will be able to “travel autonomously, unoccupied to a Tesla service center,” the company says. The fee doesn’t cover insurance.

Recent findings suggest that cybercab buyers will have other restrictions. The vehicle is for personal use only. Even though CEO Elon Musk has repeatedly stated owners will be able to put their vehicles on Tesla’s wider Robotaxi network to make money during downtime, and even has an online interest form for those who want to own and operate their own Cybercab fleets, the current ownership agreement prohibits that. Buyers are also prohibited from selling or transferring their vehicles without Tesla’s written consent. The manufacturer “advises against” children under 13 riding in the Cybercab, and prohibits children from riding without an adult present.

In a post on X, Musk showed no apparent compunction about the Cybercab business model, but did say the monthly price for autonomy “is too high.” He wrote that the price should be “more like ~$115/month.”.

NASA's Voyager 1 space probe is now one light-day away from Earth

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It traveled more than 49 years to get to this point, and its journey isn’t done yet.
  • If NASA's estimates are correct, Voyager 1 is already one light-day away from our planet.
  • "It's never happened before, and it may never happen again — it's that kind of extraordinary," stated Voyager mission manager Kareem Badaruddin.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It traveled more than 49 years to get to this point, and its journey isn’t done yet.

If NASA's estimates are correct, Voyager 1 is already one light-day away from our planet. NASA expects it to have reached that milestone at 5:16:07 AM Eastern time today, November 18. One light-day is the distance a particle of light can travel in a day. Since radio waves travel at the speed of light, it now takes 24 hours to send a command to the probe and 24 hours to get a message back. That's why NASA won't be able to confirm exactly what time it reached one light-day away until tomorrow, when the probe's message arrives.

"It's never happened before, and it may never happen again — it's that kind of extraordinary," stated Voyager mission manager Kareem Badaruddin.

Voyager 1 headed to space in 1977 as part of NASA's program to study not just our Solar System, but also interstellar space. It was launched 16 days after Voyager 2, but it has since traveled farther than its twin and any other probe we've sent out. Voyager 1 reached interstellar space — that's the region between star systems — back in 2012, before Voyager 2 did. It suffered technical glitches, and NASA had to shut down some of its features to keep it going despite the diminishing plutonium in its generator. But it's still around and hasn't stopped its journey.

It has been revealed that after traveling for 49 years, two months and 11 days, it's now believed to be about 16 billion miles from our planet—and it's not done yet. Voyager 1 is headed toward a star called Gliese 445, about 17 light-years from Earth in the Ursa Minor constellation. In terms of space distances, that's not so far away. However, none of us would be here by the time it reaches that goal: It's expected to pass within 1.7 light-years of Gliese 445 in 40,000 years.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that one reason 197,000 people, including Elon Musk, signed a petition over the weekend calling on Nvidia to reinstate the tech giant’s ousted CEO Jensen Huang is that he wasn’t just championing the AI boom. He was using Nvidia’s enormous profits to help finance it.

Industry observers note that and Nvidia has a lot of money to spend. The company reported on Tuesday net income of $64.9 billion for the third quarter, which was up from $59.7 billion the prior quarter.

But Nvidia’s continued success depends on having enough customers building and expanding data centers to keep buying its AI chips and systems. Under Huang, the manufacturer aggressively invested in AI startups and neoclouds and, more recently, began guaranteeing massive loans to finance new data centers. The biggest deal yet was the $105 billion backstop for OpenAI’s PORTS-Pike data center campus in Ohio, declared in August. In exchange for that loan guarantee, OpenAI promised that the campus would exclusively use Nvidia’s equipment, the company remarked.

Huang’s abrupt departure last week raised questions about whether Nvidia would continue bankrolling its customers at the same pace. There were reports that CFO Colette Kress, now interim CEO, had tried to push back on Huang’s increasingly ambitious dealmaking. She reportedly reduced the backstop guarantee for the OpenAI project from $250 billion down to $105 billion.

It has been revealed that under Kress, Nvidia clarified in its quarterly CFO commentary that guaranteeing a loan doesn’t mean the company is providing the financing itself. The guarantee only takes effect once the customer has secured the financing needed to build the facility and install Nvidia’s products. If the project fails to meet those conditions, the guarantee “doesn’t exist” she noted.

Sources indicate that “There is the raising of capital that they may need through equity and or debt, in order to build out any of the buildings, get them ready for use, but also the ability to procure the compute, install the compute, and get ready. What we are indicating in our statement there is that is when our guarantee starts. So if all of that begins and unfortunately they are delayed or they have a challenge in terms of building that, our guarantee doesn’t exist anymore,” Kress remarked to analysts on Tuesday during the quarterly conference call.

Industry observers note that she pointed to OpenAI PORTS-Pike campus as an example of where such terms apply. When asked, she also said this wasn’t a change in policy, but simply a clarification of existing terms. However, these disclosures have never been public before.

In a recent development, kress also made clear that Nvidia wasn’t bailing on all the ways it was financing the AI boom, especially newly introduced data centers. But, she said, Nvidia was going to be far more selective in the future.

It has been revealed that “The availability of land, power, shell is such a critical part of the whole structure in terms of building out those data centers. So they may need the assistance. That’s a great asset for anyone to hold. So we will look at that as probably one of our top priorities,” she said. At the same time, she insisted that Nvidia was “taking a very strong look in terms of the types of companies that we would want to help in terms of the financing.”.

One of the ongoing criticisms Huang faced was his love of circular deals: invest in his customers so they would turn around and buy his products. Kress is now trying to strike a delicate balance. She isn’t saying she will pull the rug out from under Nvidia’s customers. After all, the company’s investments undoubtedly spurred the AI boom that has been so lucrative for Nvidia. But she’s also signaling that the days of Huang’s freewheeling dealmaking may be over.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ahead of the busiest shopping day of the year, here’s how we determine which discounts are worth your attention.

Ahead of the busiest shopping day of the year, here’s how we determine which discounts are worth your attention.

For the past month, we’ve been inundated with Black Friday deals, signaling what’s to come on the biggest shopping day of the year in the US. We routinely get dozens of press releases a day, coming from brands substantial and small that hope that we’ll publicize these offers. Of course, the companies would prefer that we don’t do any research on these deals to see if they’re actually good, and most don’t provide any of the necessary context we’re looking for when vetting them.

Most indicators of a good deal are confusing — not just for us, but for anyone who’s shopping. Groundwork Collaborative recently published its findings about the unclear manner in which Amazon displays deals. Its researchers tracked a selection of products ahead of Black Friday and Cyber Monday in 2024 and 2025, and they claim that nearly one in three products advertised as deals on Amazon didn’t offer savings during the actual shopping events. The investigation also found that nearly a tenth of the deals it examined were more expensive during the sales events than on some days in the month leading up to them.

In a recent development, something we commonly see on Amazon and attempt to correct for in our coverage are good deals with inflated discount claims. As in, the original retail amount (the “list” price) is sometimes higher than the usual day-to-day price to make the savings seem more substantial. Sometimes, the manufacturer’s suggested retail price (MSRP) is what’s shown, though that’s not always the case.

According to recent reports, in a recent statement to investigative journalist Ronan Farrow, an unattributed Amazon spokesperson shared that its “List Price” can also be aggregated from the past 90 to 180 days of prices, not the past 30 days as Groundwork Collaborative’s research states, and is based on prices from Amazon itself and other competing retailers. However, in our experience, the confusing way pricing and discounts are communicated isn’t limited to Amazon.

Recent findings suggest that the group’s findings show how easy it is to distrust the prices you see, especially online, where dynamic pricing sometimes comes into play. Regardless of retailer practices, we understand the importance of curating what you see on The Verge with care.

In a recent development, vetting deals for coverage consideration is a big, albeit invisible, part of our jobs, even outside of big shopping events. Most of what we’re pitched day to day, or what we see in our respective feeds, never hits the site because it doesn’t meet our standards. Even when the deal is for a product we’ve tested and really enjoy — our north star for what to cover on the deals front — that alone doesn’t guarantee coverage. We often skip covering deals that aren’t as good as a retailer or brand made them seem. Or maybe the deal is good, but it returns every week, lasts only a few hours, or it’s available only with a premium membership. Alternatively, the deal might only be available from a retailer none of us has heard of or shopped at. Needless to say, we consider a ton of factors.

Recent findings suggest that with Black Friday coming up, you deserve transparency from us so you know — whether it’s this month or a random day in February — that you’re looking at an actual deal when you visit our site. The most basic criteria we use to judge whether a deal is good is whether we like the product enough to write about it and whether its price has dropped. Then we assess whether the discount is actually worth your attention. That part of the conversation has become a little complicated in the past year. RAMageddon and the ripple effects of higher tariffs have, in some cases, substantially impacted pricing and, by extension, the deals we cover.

We follow deals closely enough to know when to bite at an offer or let it pass.

For products hit by recent price hikes, the upcoming deal prices sometimes amount to the original sticker price, or close to it. Several of us would nod our heads with you if you think, “Hey, that’s not a deal; that’s just the original price. I’m no fool!” But it’s also technically a deal for many of us who are just trying to save wherever possible. Along those lines, we’ll sometimes highlight ways to save on digital or physical goods by buying discounted gift cards, which can be used to buy in-demand products. These methods are the only way to get any kind of deal on Grand Theft Auto VI before launch, for example.

To help us stay aware of price drops, we also use free tracking tools like CamelCamelCamel and Keepa, which provide an independent read on Amazon’s historical pricing. (You can use them, too!) They’ll alert us when a product we like — and that we know you’ll probably like — goes on sale. Amazon also has its own Alexa for Shopping tool, which can show up to a year of pricing data and perform several other AI chatbot-like actions, including automatically buying products on your behalf. In my experience, Amazon’s historical pricing data usually aligns with non-Amazon-affiliated companies. However, none of them are perfect. Even the third-party tools we use don’t always display the record-low prices we’ve covered, for whatever reason. All of this to say, there are a lot of ins and outs, but we follow deals closely enough to know when to bite at an offer or let it pass.

We cast a fairly large net for products across a range of categories ahead of the holidays, including some that don’t often get much play on The Verge. However, of the thousands of deals that we’ve seen ahead of Black Friday, you’re seeing the mere dozens of standouts that we’ve tested or used in our personal lives within each category — headphones, TVs, gaming accessories, smart home tech, etc. — that meet our criteria for being good products at noteworthy prices.

The digital version is 212GB in size and would take more than an hour to download for those with a 1Gbps internet connection. Rockstar Games has also rolled out pre-release patches since GTA VI became available for pre-order, with the latest one being 600 MB. The patches should automatically download for those who've already preloaded the game.

TL;DR: Pokémon GO and Duolingo just teamed up for exclusive cross-app rewards. Score free Duolingo avatar suits, regional and shiny encounters, and more.

Pokémon GO and Duolingo just merged forces in one of the most delightfully chaotic app crossovers of the year.

According to recent reports, live from Nov. 17, the two mobile giants are running a cross-app event called Duo’s Pokémon Party. By keeping a seven-day language streak alive in Duolingo, players can unlock custom Pokémon outfits for their Duolingo avatars alongside a unique promo code for event-themed Timed Research in Pokémon GO.

To join, trainers must opt into Duo’s Pokémon Party inside the Duolingo app by Dec. 21, and finish at least one lesson per day across seven separate days before Dec. 29. It's that easy.

It has been revealed that maybe we're cynical, but this feels like a rare opportunity. It's refreshing to see a free cross-promotion that rewards daily habits across both platforms:.

Four free Duolingo avatar suits: Completing daily lessons unlocks up to nine total rewards, headlined by four wearable Pokémon suits for your Duolingo profile: Pikachu, Chatot, a Poké Ball, and a Pokémon GO trainer outfit.

Sources indicate that regional and Shiny encounters in Pokémon GO: Finishing seven days of lessons generates a unique offer code redeemable on the Pokémon GO Web Store. That unlocks Timed Research featuring XP, Stardust, and guaranteed encounters with Pikachu, Meowth, Lucario, and regional-exclusive Chatot.

Foreign-language gameplay and fresh language tags: When you activate the Timed Research, you pick a target language, and your tasks actually appear in that language. Caught Pokémon also debut a new Language Tag on their summary screen, letting you tap to inspect their official names across different languages.

We should note that while the Pokémon GO encounters are permanent additions to your Pokédex, the four Pokémon avatar suits are temporary rentals. All earned Pokémon suits will automatically expire and vanish from your Duolingo closet on March 31, 2027.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google Voice is a wonderful service that’s often neglected, but with RCS supposedly on the way, a upcoming app redesign is now rolling out on Android that might as well have a big neon sign that indicates “RCS is coming.”.

Industry observers note that google Voice is a US-only service that operates a phone number over the internet. No normal carrier, just an app tied to your Google account that gets a phone number with the ability to make calls and send/receive text messages. The latter, though, has been a point of contention for the past few years as Voice was excluded from Google’s huge push into RCS.

According to recent reports, that might finally be changing, though. Recent updates brought mention of RCS in the app’s code.

Now, a slightly newer version (v2026-11-01-1019342246) of Google Voice has debuted a redesign for the app on Android.

The latest look isn’t a drastic restructuring, but a huge coat of paint on an app that hasn’t seen any meaningful updates since 2023. The new look feels more modern and very much influenced by Google Messages. The text field at the bottom has a rounded design with the same “+” and camera icons found in Messages, as well as a new long-press gesture that is, again, similar to Google’s primary messaging app. The main page hasn’t been updated beyond a new, rounded search bar up top and some subtly bolder fonts.

Material You colors are hit or miss now. On a Pixel with an orange theme, that color influenced the entire UI, but on a Galaxy Z Fold 8 with a coral/blue theme, the only sign of themeing was a blue message field.

Sources indicate that the most key thing here is the “SMS” icon on the send button, which looks just like the button in Google Messages. In that app, it’s used as an indicator as to what type of message you’re sending – SMS or RCS. Combined with code in that other recent patch directly pointing to “RCS” being used on a send button, you can absolutely tell Google Voice is finally adding this long-overdue functionality.

A timeline for RCS support in Google Voice is still unclear, but this redesign going live now certainly suggests it’s coming sooner rather than later.

How to hide the newly introduced macOS 27.3 menu bar indicator

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (324 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that macOS 27.3 beta 2 adds a blue menu bar indicator for apps using System & App Protection Override.
  • Sources indicate that if you regularly use trusted automation tools and utilities, that can mean a persistent pill taking up space in your menu bar.
  • I’ve tested this on macOS 27.3 beta 2 and confirmed that the indicator disappears after a restart.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that macOS 27.3 beta 2 adds a blue menu bar indicator for apps using System & App Protection Override. Apple describes itas a transparency indicator that appears when one app is controlling another.

Sources indicate that if you regularly use trusted automation tools and utilities, that can mean a persistent pill taking up space in your menu bar. Prefer to hide it? There’s a Terminal workaround.

I’ve tested this on macOS 27.3 beta 2 and confirmed that the indicator disappears after a restart.

Open Terminal and run these two commands:.

sudo mkdir -p /Library/Preferences/FeatureFlags/Domainsudo defaults write /Library/Preferences/FeatureFlags/Domain/TCC AX_TRANSPARENCY_INDICATOR -dict Enabled -bool false.

Enter your Mac administrator password when prompted, then restart your Mac.

In a recent development, the command disables the internal AX_TRANSPARENCY_INDICATOR feature flag. It doesn’t remove apps from your permissions list, although you’ll no longer see this activity indicator.

To restore Apple’s default behavior, run:.

sudo defaults delete /Library/Preferences/FeatureFlags/Domain/TCC AX_TRANSPARENCY_INDICATOR.

Restart your Mac again to apply the reversal. This removes only the indicator override, preserving any other flags you may have configured.

This is an undocumented workaround tested on the current beta, so Apple could change or remove it in a future enhancement.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • If you've asked yourself this question, or have peered lustfully at the upcoming foldable phones, including from Apple, you should take a look at the new Xiaomi 18 Pro or 18 Pro Max.
  • Sources indicate that I've spent a few days with both phones, and I can tell you, these are incredibly fast, capable, and sleek devices, albeit a little iPhone-like.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What if your phone had a second display on the back?

If you've asked yourself this question, or have peered lustfully at the upcoming foldable phones, including from Apple, you should take a look at the new Xiaomi 18 Pro or 18 Pro Max. The display is very cool and does bring some functionality that you otherwise just cannot have, though it's not nearly as versatile as what you get with a foldable phone.

Sources indicate that I've spent a few days with both phones, and I can tell you, these are incredibly fast, capable, and sleek devices, albeit a little iPhone-like. The display on the back is what makes them stand out from the crowd, at least visually, but it's not something that will drastically change the way you use your phone.

It has been revealed that the Xiaomi 18 Pro series is not Xiaomi's first phone to feature a secondary display on the back; last year's Xiaomi 17 Pro had one, too. Just like the main display on the front, it hasn't changed much since last year: It's still a 2.9-inch, 596x976 pixel AMOLED display, though it is a little brighter than before. I didn't get to try the 17 Pro, though, so the display on the back is fresh to me.

Displays: 6.9-inch, 1,208x2,624 pixel, 120Hz AMOLED display with 4000 nits of peak brightness; secondary display on the back: 2.9-inch, 120Hz AMOLED display with 4000 nits of peak brightness.

Design: Dragon Crystal Glass 3 front, aluminum frame,.

Size and weight: 163.4 x 77.6 x 8.4 mm; weight: 240 grams.

Rear cameras: A triple rear camera system with a 200-megapixel, f/1.7 wide camera, a 200-megapixel, f/2.4 periscope telephoto camera, and a 50-megapixel, f/2.4 ultrawide camera.

Front cameras: 50-megapixel, f/2.2 selfie camera.

Processor: Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6.

Storage: 256GB/512GB/1TB with 12/16GB of RAM.

Battery life: 7,050mAh battery with 100W charging, 50 wireless, and 27W reverse wireless charging.

Software: Android 17, HyperOS 4.

Water and dust resistance: IP68 rating.

Special features: Under display ultrasonic fingerprint scanner, stereo audio system with 3 speakers, 24-bit/192kHz hi-res audio support.

Yes, this is an extremely powerful phone, even though it isn't technically Xiaomi's flagship (that's the Ultra series, which isn't out yet this year). You get the latest Snapdragon chip, a massive camera upgrade over last year's 50-megapixel system, and a humongous battery that charges very promptly.

The Xiaomi 18 Pro, which I also received for testing but have spent less time with, has a 6.4-inch display, a smaller battery, with the rest being mostly the same.

Industry observers note that xiaomi flagships in the numbered series follow the same philosophy: Make a phone that's very much like an iPhone, but stuff it with extremely powerful hardware for added value. It starts with the phones' names (18 Pro and 18 Pro Max), it's visible in parts of the design, and Xiaomi's HyperOS, which has been upgraded to version 4 here, can be set up to mirror iOS in almost every way.

This is not a bad thing. The Xiaomi 18 Pro is distinctive enough with its dual display that overall iPhone-likeness doesn't feel like you're having a cheap copy. And I don't mind the HyperOS software being a dead ringer for iOS, down to the near-identical Control Center (which, you guessed it, is called the Control Center on the Xiaomi as well).

Recent findings suggest that do I need a display on the back of the phone? Not really. It's useful for photos as it can give cues to the folks you're photographing, and it can take your selfies game to the next level as you can actually take selfies with the 200-megapixel main camera system. Other than that, it just looks cool.

Recent findings suggest that but you do need to see it in real life to appreciate just how cool it is. It's an excellent, super-bright, pixel-dense AMOLED display with a 120Hz refresh rate. I set it up with an ocean wave animation that looks downright beautiful when I touch it. You can have AI-based apps on there, and even use it for simple games. It's so good that I kept consciously placing the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max on its face when setting it on a table, just to appreciate the crispness of that mini display on the back.

According to recent reports, but other than the camera tricks, it's still (surprise!) preferable to use the much larger front display for most tasks. The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile.

And yes, the 6.9-inch front display is excellent, too: Silky smooth, plenty bright, and it even has a Privacy Display option, similar to the one on recent Samsung flagships.

In a recent development, up until a few years ago, battery capacities north of 5,000mAh were reserved for thick specialty phones focusing on battery life. But then a couple of battery breakthroughs (including silicon-carbon battery tech which Xiaomi is using here) made it to the mass market, and now Xiaomi can place an 7,050mAh battery in the regular-sized Xiaomi 18 Pro Max.

Recent findings suggest that the battery charges promptly on a fast charger and it lasts for at least two days. It's so good that I didn't have proper time to really test it as I only charged the phone twice in little under a week.

I don't think I've ever used a Xiaomi phone that was as quick and worked as smoothly as this one. Everything I touched opened instantly (including the fingerprint scanner which takes a tiny fraction of a second to analyze your digit and log you in). Playing with animated, AI-based and fancy perspective wallpapers did not punish me in terms of speed, as the phone kept operating incredibly smoothly.

Yes, it has the latest Snapdragon chip inside, but I guess Xiaomi also polished its HyperOS 4 to make it a little speedier than before.

In a recent development, as is customary for Xiaomi, HyperOS does have a maddening number of features and options, some of which are tucked away in some menu you wouldn't think of. But given the versatility of this phone, it's hard to blame them. One I set the phone up as I liked, the complexity of the Settings did not bother me.

We've gotten to a point in which Xiaomi can put two 200-megapixel cameras, and a two 50-megapixel ones on a phone that's not really their camera flagship.

According to recent reports, do we need so many megapixels? Possibly not, as evidenced in the fact that Xiaomi 18 Pro Max takes 12.5 megapixel photos by default, and you have to manually up the resolution to either 50 or 200 megapixels.

But the high megapixel count opens up interesting possibilities, such as zooming in at 12.8x without losing quality. The telephoto camera doubles as a macro camera that can go in really close (its minimum focusing distance is 12 centimetres), with Xiaomi calling it a "telescope and microscope in one.".

According to recent reports, I haven't had enough time with the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max's camera to fully assess how good it is. From what I've seen, though, it's an incredibly versatile and powerful system that you can use to squeeze out a good photo in almost every scenario.

Sources indicate that the Xiaomi 18 Pro starts at 1,399 EUR, while the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max starts at 1,599 EUR in Europe. The colors on offer are Cosmic Blue, Black, White, and Velvet Red for both devices. We don't have the exact date of availability yet, and will upgrade this article when we get them.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After testing a rumored $499/month subscription tier, gay hookup app Grindr is officially launching Edge, an AI-focused plan running for $120 a month in the U.S. or $70 per week.

Edge has three main features: Insights, which reveals consumers compatibility and likelihood to reply; Recommendations, which provides five curated profiles a day; and Reconnect (called A-List in beta), which highlights past connections and generates summaries of your conversations.

Edge includes everything that's in Grindr's Unlimited subscription, as well, which includes features like being able to scroll through unlimited profiles, incognito mode, unsending messages, and expiring photos.

AdultFriendFinder — readers’ pick for casual connections.

Tinder — top pick for fast hookups.

Hinge — popular choice for regular meetups.

Pure — best for anonymous hookups.

OkCupid — best app for inclusivity.

Edge is powered by Grindr's proprietary AI stack called "gAI." Consumers can control which sensitive data to provide gAI and whether the app can use this to develop gAI over time. Such data can include preferred position, ethnicity, and user chats.

Grindr states that certain health data won't be used in gAI, like HIV status, last tested date, testing reminders, the "Poz" tribe and tag (which stands for the HIV-positive community), and vaccination status. Grindr recently settled a lawsuit for £26 million after allegedly sharing users' HIV statuses with third parties. (Grindr denied the allegations.) Shortly after, the app acquired a provider of the HIV-prevention medication PrEP, and plans to provide PrEP on the app.

Mashable received an early demo of Edge last week, during which Grindr's chief product officer, AJ Balance, mentioned that Edge is the app's most personalized experience yet.

It has been revealed that balance remarked that Grindr people are at the forefront of culture and tech, and the Grindr team believes it's their job to leverage fresh technology. As AI was unfolding and it was clear it was the next paradigm shift, Grindr saw an opportunity to utilize it to add value to its users' lives.

Sources indicate that enthusiasm for Edge was apparently high during beta testing, Balance told Mashable, and beta testers ultimately want more connection with less effort and reduced friction in finding a match. The blog post Balance penned for the release is even called, "More Action, Less Effort.".

What about the alleged $499/month price tag for the subscription?

Balance remarked that the app tested a range of pricing. And while $120 is much less than $499, Grindr CEO George Arison defended the price to BBC News today, saying that, "I think we're a capitalist society, and everything hinges on whether you can afford it or not." Balance told Mashable that 91 percent of its people use the app for free, while the remaining 9 percent are power users who want more convenience and ease to save time.

Edge is now available globally to all Grindr users on iOS and Android.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, meta is testing Direct, a new stand-alone messaging app that houses Instagram’s direct messages. Direct is initially launching in Turkey and Thailand, and can be used with or without an Instagram account.

With Direct, Meta is likely looking to retain owners who use Instagram primarily, or even exclusively, for messaging. Over the years, people have often sought various ways to use Instagram’s direct messaging features without having to deal with the rest of the platform.

Direct appears to be Meta’s answer to that demand, as the tech giant claims it is designed for chatting one-on-one or in groups with friends and family.

The fresh app also gives the company a way to keep these owners within its ecosystem rather than risk losing them altogether, and count them as active users within its ecosystem, even if they don’t use Instagram itself.

Besides usual messaging features like reactions, voice notes, and emojis, Direct also features a “Draw” feature that lets you doodle and sketch directly inside chat threads. There’s also “Notes,” which are the short status updates that appear at the top of your Instagram DMs.

Meta says customers can create custom stickers, add audio effects to replies, and personalize chat backgrounds with custom themes.

In a recent development, meta says only people in your contacts or those you’re already connected with can start conversations or add you to group chats. Users can also report, block, restrict, or remove contacts at any time.

In a recent development, the manufacturer also says it will use its age-estimation technology to identify and address potentially inappropriate interactions involving young users. Parents will also have access to supervision tools that let them see who their teens are messaging, manage safety settings, and set daily usage limits.

Teens who use their Instagram username and password to access Direct will have to work with all the same messaging restrictions as Instagram’s Teen Accounts.

Meta did not say when or if it will bring Direct to additional countries.

Recent findings suggest that drone and missile strikes have inflicted unprecedented damage on data centers in Eastern Europe and the Middle East this year, disrupting cloud services for millions of people and permanently deleting some Amazon Web Services customer data. This trend represents a latest concern for Substantial Tech companies—but also for governments and everyone else who depends on common digital services in modern life.

To explore what this all means for modern society’s reliance on cloud resilience, I will be hosting a live conversation titled “Drone attacks and data centers: Latest Risks for Big Tech” on Tuesday, November 17 at 1 pm ET with Joseph Jarnecki, a senior research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), a UK defense and security think tank. He leads RUSI’s work on how cloud services factor into national security and defense, along with tech sovereignty efforts.

Jarnecki has done extensive research on how Ukraine strengthened its cloud resilience with Western partners despite facing both cyberattacks and kinetic attacks at the start of the full-scale Russian invasion, and explored what that means for NATO and European governments’ cloud adoption looks.

This year, Jarnecki has written about Iran’s drone and missile strikes on Amazon data centers in the Middle East during the US-Israeli war with Iran, and the broader implications for governments and Significant Tech. He has also commented on the impacts of Russia and Ukraine exchanging strikes on each other’s data centers.

For more background on the data center attacks that have transpired so far in 2026, you can see my previous Ars coverage of how the Iranian strikes left Amazon with months of repairs, and caused enough damage to result in the permanent loss of some AWS customer data.

I’ve also covered why Russia was not ready for the data center war it started with Ukraine, with the systematic Russian strike campaign targeting Ukraine’s data centers provoking Ukrainian counterstrikes that damaged Russian government data centers and AI data centers owned by the Russian tech giant Yandex.

My conversation with Jarnecki will explore why data centers have become much more prominent military targets, whether defending or hardening data centers against drones and missiles is a realistic option, how cloud resiliency can be improved in wartime conditions, and the choices governments and cloud providers face in deploying data centers during an era of growing geopolitical risks.

In a recent development, you can watch the discussion live on YouTube on November 17 at 1 pm ET. We will also be fielding a few audience questions.

  • Uber Eats customers in a Houston suburb can now have their food delivered by a Zipline drone, the first commercial launch under a partnership announced earlier this year between Uber and the autonomous drone delivery startup.
  • According to recent reports, the commercial partnership kicks off Tuesday in Spring, Texas, before expanding to Dallas.
  • Sources indicate that zipline’s long-range autonomous delivery drones will be used to shuttle food orders weighing up to eight pounds to Uber Eats customers, flying about 300 feet above the ground at speeds of up to 70 miles per hour.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Uber Eats customers in a Houston suburb can now have their food delivered by a Zipline drone, the first commercial launch under a partnership announced earlier this year between Uber and the autonomous drone delivery startup.

According to recent reports, the commercial partnership kicks off Tuesday in Spring, Texas, before expanding to Dallas. But the companies have far larger ambitions. Uber and Zipline blueprint to launch drone delivery services in dozens of additional U.S. cities in their collective bid to make one million deliveries per day using the startup’s drones by the end of 2029.

Sources indicate that zipline’s long-range autonomous delivery drones will be used to shuttle food orders weighing up to eight pounds to Uber Eats customers, flying about 300 feet above the ground at speeds of up to 70 miles per hour. Zipline drones don’t land. Instead, the drones lower the orders, which are encased in a small protective pod, to the customer’s location using a tether.

Uber Eats customers in service areas will be able to tap a new “drone” icon on the app’s home page to view all participating restaurants. Uber said that at launch in the Houston area, several nationwide chains, including Jersey Mike’s and Zaxby’s, along with dozens of local restaurants such as Urban Bird and Abu Omar Halal, will offer drone delivery.

“In partnership with Uber Eats we’re going to create a latest expectation for delivery in America,” Zipline CEO and co-founder Keller Cliffton noted in a statement that underscores those aspirations.

Sources indicate that those nationwide goals mirror the ambitions of other drone delivery companies, including Alphabet-owned Wing and Amazon’s Prime Air service. And those prepares have started to collide with concerns from residents in some locations who complain about noise and worry that the drones will disrupt wildlife and pose a risk to safety and privacy.

Companies trying to scale in this nascent industry have argued that delivery via drone is a net benefit for society, citing advantages such as traffic reduction. Customers won’t need to hop in their cars and drive to the store for that forgotten item or takeout order, instead relying on a drone, industry proponents have remarked.

And while Zipline and other companies have been developing their drones for years, the industry is still in its early days, as is adoption in the communities where services are available.

In a recent development, zipline, which was founded in 2014, has developed a drone delivery ecosystem that includes aircraft, launch and landing systems, and logistics software. The California-based company’s initial focus was delivering blood in Rwanda, but it eventually expanded its scope to the United States. Its business in the U.S. scaled swiftly after receiving its Part 135 air carrier certification from the Federal Aviation Administration in 2022, a critical regulatory hurdle that authorized the company to conduct long-range commercial drone deliveries.

In a recent development, uber’s partnership extends beyond a commercial relationship with Zipline. The ride-hailing giant also invested in the startup. Neither firm has disclosed the investment amount, but Zipline declared last week it had raised $1.5 billion in a round led by Paradigm, WCM Investment Management, and Layer Global, and included backing by Uber, among others.

  • The Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) and the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) are conducting a scheduled test of the national emergency alert system at 2:20 p.m.
  • The FCC released a public notice about the scheduled test on Sept.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you hear an emergency broadcast this afternoon, don't panic!

The Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) and the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) are conducting a scheduled test of the national emergency alert system at 2:20 p.m. ET on Tuesday, Nov. 17.

The FCC released a public notice about the scheduled test on Sept. 16, but it comes at a moment of high national anxiety, driven by recent tech outages — among other troubling news stories.

First, Microsoft suffered a widespread global outage on Thursday, Nov. 12, followed by a rare FAA nationwide ground stoppage the following day. And on Monday, a JPMorgan Chase outage sparked reports of a major bank outage (the problem was limited to Chase Bank and not a systemic glitch or the result of a cyberattack), followed quickly by a United Airlines outage.

None of these outages were directly related to or caused by cyberattackers, but the timing has sparked conspiracy theories and generalized anxiety.

However, the emergency alert was scheduled long before these outages; the FCC also announced a backup date of Dec. 3, in the event today's test does not occur. So, if your TV or radio suddenly goes into emergency mode today, don't freak out.

In a recent development, FEMA will use the Integrated Public Alert and Warning System (IPAWS) to disseminate a message in both English and Spanish. The message will read, "This is a nationwide test of the Emergency Alert System, issued by the Federal Emergency Management Agency, covering the United States from 2:20 to 2:50 hours ET. This is only a test. No action is required by the public.".

The test will appear on the following types of media:.

Wired and wireless cable television systems.

Digital television broadcast stations.

Digital audio broadcasting systems.

Notably, the emergency alert will not appear on your phone. So, if you do receive an "emergency alert" by text or phone this afternoon, ignore it; scammers may be trying to take advantage of the test.

FEMA tests emergency text alerts, or Wireless Emergency Alerts (WEA), separately.

Outside of testing, WEA notifications are used for Imminent Threat alerts, Amber Alerts, Public Safety Messages (PSAs), and National Alerts, which are issued by the president or the FEMA administrator.

Industry observers note that after we missed out on the Xiaomi 17 Pro and Pro Max last year, the Chinese smartphone giant is finally bringing its dual-screen flagships to the West. It's just launched the latest Xiaomi 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max, and I would be pretty worried if I were a certain Cupertino-based competitor.

Both phones look like an all-round excellent package, with top-of-the-line specs including the brand-fresh Snapdragon 8 Elite chipsets.

According to recent reports, the Xiaomi 18 Pro is the model for those after a more compact, but still powerful, phone, with its 6.4-inch 120Hz AMOLED front display and 6,000mAh battery. It's powered by the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 chipset, paired with 12GB of RAM and either 256GB or 512GB of storage.

Recent findings suggest that the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max, meanwhile, bumps the main screen size up to 6.9 inches and upgrades the chipset to the absolutely top-of-the-line Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 – currently the fastest Android SoC on the market. The base model offers 12GB of RAM and 256GB of storage, but there are also more expensive 12+512GB and 16+1TB versions available.

The bigger design also makes space for a much larger battery, which comes in at 7,050mAh with 100W wired HyperCharge support (the base 18 Pro, in contrast, only supports 90W wired HyperCharge).

The front displays of both phones support Xiaomi's new privacy display technology, which is effectively the organization's take on Samsung's Privacy Display feature and helps obscure sensitive information from prying eyes.

Both the 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max boast similar camera setups, with a 200MP main shooter and 200MP periscope telephoto lens alongside a 50MP ultra-wide. As with other recent Xiaomi devices, the cameras were co-engineered with Leica and offer a range of photo styles inspired by the camera maker.

Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android.

Recent findings suggest that for me, the real highlight, however, is the innovative rear display situated on the back of both models. It offers a range of handy features, from controlling media playback to offering a real-time view of the cameras to make selfies easier.

You can fully customize it with a range of watch-like faces as well (including some options with cute 3D animal mascots) and even use generative AI to create your own apps right from the settings menu.

It's seriously cool and seems like a genuine reason to pick the 18 Pro or 18 Pro Max over other flagship models.

All of this doesn't exactly come cheap, however. The Xiaomi 18 Pro starts at £1,199 (that's roughly $1,600), and the 18 Pro Max starts at £1,399 (around $1,850) for the 12+256GB model.

They both come in four color options: Black, White, Velvet Red, and Cosmic Blue.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that can an AI agent serve as your personal stylist?
  • On Tuesday, the company launched “Daydream Agent,” an AI agent that is described as a personal stylist that can help you proposal a look, virtually try on clothes, surface relevant pieces based on your taste, and more.
  • The idea, the company explains, is to put a personal stylist in everyone’s pocket.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that can an AI agent serve as your personal stylist? That’s what e-commerce veteran Julie Bornstein’s fashion startup, Daydream, aims to find out.

On Tuesday, the company launched “Daydream Agent,” an AI agent that is described as a personal stylist that can help you proposal a look, virtually try on clothes, surface relevant pieces based on your taste, and more.

The idea, the company explains, is to put a personal stylist in everyone’s pocket. This application of AI could be promising, given that early adopters of consumer AI agents like Meta’s Muse have found that online shopping is a key use case.

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg recently noted that shopping was a top activity for Muse’s over 10 million owners and that 25% of people who set up Muse now use it daily.

It has been revealed that in Daydream’s case, the fashion startup has been focused on using AI to deliver personalized shopping results to its owners. Its new AI agent builds on its earlier work with an AI chatbot that could help users find outfits and make suggestions, but not complete purchases.

In a recent development, now the firm says its Daydream Agent expands on that experience by remembering each shopper’s own personal style, fit preferences, and budget to refine its recommendations. Shoppers can also upload a photo to have the agent reuse that image to virtually try on any item they’ve saved. When they find something they like, the agent can complete a purchase through a one-click checkout process.

The agent can also handle other fashion-related tasks, like keeping an eye on when items go on sale or when brands have a new drop, or providing weekly updates or spotting new fashion trends.

Also, instead of leaving items in their cart, shoppers can save pieces they’re interested in to a persistent “clothing rack” so they can compare options and think about their purchases before deciding what to buy. Shoppers can also connect their own closet and their calendar to the agent, helping them to build outfits around what they already own and plan what to wear for upcoming events.

It has been revealed that the tech works by pulling real-time pricing and availability information from its catalog of over 10,000 brands, then combines that with its fashion-focused artificial intelligence. It’s powered by a combination of OpenAI, Gemini, and Claude models, which it fine-tuned, along with its own trained models designed for particular use cases.

Sources indicate that however, considering that fashion is more of an art than a science, the firm says it’s keeping humans in the loop. To do so, this month it brought on its first stylist in residence, Francesca Salih, an international fashion stylist and the founder of StyleGrid. Salih provides the startup with styling content that helps shape how the agent pulls together outfits and offers advice. This advice is part of the company’s fashion knowledge database, which the agent experience relies on.

Bornstein, formerly Stitch Fix’s COO and the founder of The Yes (exited to Pinterest in 2022), started Daydream in 2023 as an AI search engine. The organization, backed by $50 million in funding from Forerunner Ventures, Index Ventures, GV, and True Ventures, says more than 2 million shoppers have used Daydream to discover apparel and accessories since its June 2025 launch.

Google Pixel Tag review: Simple but effective

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1221 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Google’s take on Apple’s AirTag is a basic but still valuable tool for Android people.
  • We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
  • There was a time in my life when I thought tracking gadgets were a waste of resources.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google’s take on Apple’s AirTag is a basic but still valuable tool for Android people.

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

There was a time in my life when I thought tracking gadgets were a waste of resources. But after having kids and getting older, I've come around on the category. Sometimes it's just nice to hand off the mental load of keeping tabs on various objects or to have a better way of finding misplaced items that isn't just retracing your footsteps. It's not a terribly complex task, but if a tracker isn't reliable and easy to use, it won't be much help when you need it most. With the new $30 Pixel Tag, Google has created its version of Apple's AirTag to give Android phone users a simple and straightforward way of finding lost items and preventing the fear of things going missing in the first place.

There's not much going on with the Pixel Tag's exterior. It features a pill-shaped plastic and metal housing that's about the size and weight of two quarters arranged side by side. There's a tiny opening in front for its built-in speaker and around back there's a removable cover that gives you access to its replaceable coin-cell battery. Right below the cover, there's also a hidden button that you can double press to ring your phone, but only if you remember to opt-in to that feature inside Google's Find Hub app.

Recent findings suggest that the whole thing is pretty sleek and it's small enough that you can stash it almost anywhere, allowing you to add tracking capabilities to all sorts of things like bags, wallets, keys or even water bottles (just remember not to put it in the dishwasher). It even has an IP67 rating for dust and water resistance, so you won't need to worry about how it will fare in harsher outdoor conditions. Unfortunately, there isn't a small keyring loop on the device itself, so unless the object you want to track has a small pocket for holding the Pixel Tag, you may need to resort to third-party cases (like the one from Bellroy I've been using) in order to attach it to your valuables.

Initial setup for the Pixel Tag couldn't be easier. All you have to do is put it next to your phone and remove the little tab sticking out from behind its battery cover. This turns it on and after that, you'll see a little notification on your phone to finish the onboarding process, which includes pointing you to the Play Store to download the Find Hub app (assuming it isn't installed already).

From there, you can give the Pixel Tag a proper name, specify what it's going to be tracking and then you're pretty much good to go. If the tracker is attached to an item used by multiple people, you have the option of sharing ownership inside the app, so everyone can see where it is. You can also tell the app to notify you when you leave something behind, to prevent you from getting all the way home before realizing that your bag is still, say, at the restaurant. And naturally, there's also a handy map that will show you exactly where the tracker was last seen, powered by Google's Find Hub network and the millions of participating Android devices that help the Pixel Tag triangulate its location.

In the event that your Pixel Tag and the object it's attached to go missing, you can press a button in the app to make the tracker play a sound. Alternatively, you can also hit the Find Nearby function to launch a mode that will help you hone in on the device's location. For people with phones that support ultra wideband, you'll sometimes even get an extra level of accuracy that includes little arrows on the screen to prevent your search from turning into a game of Hot or Cold.

That remarked, it's not 100 percent bulletproof, because I noticed that after I asked my son to hide the Pixel Tag somewhere in our home, I wasn't always able to see the on-screen arrows (or sometimes they would be pointing the wrong direction) when searching for it, which I attribute to stuff like walls and furniture causing interference with its tracking capabilities. Still, it was always good enough to get me in the right ballpark and from there I simply had it play a sound to finally nail down the tag's position.

According to recent reports, for further testing, I asked my wife to stash the tag in her purse while she went to a doctor's appointment and it worked great then too, even over much longer distances. However, I did notice that Google has included some welcome privacy features, which includes the tag giving her phone a notification that there might be a device following her. I also discovered that when she was in a car, the Pixel Tag's location was much slower to revision in real time, but in my view, that's a feature not a bug. This thing isn't meant to spy on other people, so I appreciate that there are built-in precautions for anyone trying to use it for that.

And if you do genuinely lose the tracker (and presumably the item it's attached to), you can mark it as lost, allowing you to pin a phone number, message and an email, so that if a good samaritan finds it, they'll be able to see that info on their phone and have the ability to reach out and return it.

The Pixel Tag has been on sale for less than a month, so there's no real way to properly test its longevity at this time. But Google notes its single coin cell provides up to a full year of battery life, which is similar to an AirTag though a bit less than Samsung's latest Galaxy SmartTag 3 (550 days in normal mode). Thankfully, if it does run out of juice, you don't need to throw it away as you can easily replace its lone CR2032 cell.

Industry observers note that the Pixel Tag isn't super flashy, but it does everything you'd expect from a low-cost tracker. You can extend ownership with family members to make keeping track of shared items a breeze and Google's Find Hub network provides an accurate way of locating something no matter where it is. If something gets misplaced, you can easily track it down via the app or just by telling the tag to play a sound. It also works in reverse too, because you can just press the button on its back to ring your handset, which can be really helpful when your toddler decides it's time to play hide and seek with daddy's phone. Its biggest shortcoming is when you compare it to Samsung's Galaxy SmartTag 3, which has an extra level of activity tracking for keeping tabs on pets and a deeper level of support for geofencing. But for all the Android device consumers out there, if all you want is a simple, no-nonsense tracker for rapidly locating your gear, the Pixel Tag is exactly what you need. I just wish there was an easier way to attach it to things without needing extra accessories.

House Democrats promise a US return to global climate talks

💡 Key Takeaways
  • ANTALYA, Turkey—After their massive gains in the 2026 midterm elections, a delegation of Democratic US House members appeared at the United Nations COP31 climate change conference Monday, pledging to rejoin the international fight against global warming.
  • Jared Huffman (D-Calif.), ranking member of the House Natural Resources Committee, remarked it is a “pivotal time” for US climate and energy policy.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

ANTALYA, Turkey—After their massive gains in the 2026 midterm elections, a delegation of Democratic US House members appeared at the United Nations COP31 climate change conference Monday, pledging to rejoin the international fight against global warming.

Sources indicate that rep. Jared Huffman (D-Calif.), ranking member of the House Natural Resources Committee, remarked it is a “pivotal time” for US climate and energy policy.

“The wrecking ball of Donald Trump and this out-of-touch administration, and the temporarily empty chair of the United States at this COP31, does not represent what the Americans want or need,” Huffman noted.

In a recent development, president Donald Trump has pulled the United States out of the Paris climate agreement twice and is trying to quit the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change. The current administration has also tried to cut all funding for climate programs.

Since Trump returned to the White House in 2025, the United States has had no formal government presence at the UN talks, but was informally represented by America Is All In, a coalition including local governments, businesses, faith groups, Native American tribes, and universities.

Huffman remarked the midterm election demonstrates that Americans have rejected the current administration’s efforts to “turn the United States into something like a petro-dictatorship.” The results could pave the way for the country to reestablish a formal presence at the annual talks.

Given legal uncertainties about Trump’s efforts to completely withdraw the US from the UN’s climate framework, the extent of US participation in the talks is unclear. But Huffman stated that, in the past, US congressional delegations have attended the annual Conference of the Parties, as the meeting is formally known, under both Democratic and Republican majorities.

“The next time we’re here, we will be an official congressional delegation led by the leadership of the House of Representatives,” Huffman noted in an interview with Inside Climate News.

The US would still be excluded from the formal government-to-government negotiations, but a congressional delegation representing the majority party, potentially capable of advancing climate and energy legislation, could make a difference, Huffman noted.

“We want to take the best practices that we’ve heard from all of the global partners… and craft them into good, solid climate policy once we get back to Congress,” said Rep. Lucy McBath (D-Ga.).

Recent findings suggest that the new Democratic majority in the House of Representatives can also use its oversight authority to try to ensure that the money the US has promised for climate aid and sustainable development is restored, said U.S. Rep. Sean Casten (D-Ill.).

Casten remarked some of America’s European allies are “spending $500, $600 million per day more than before the United States attacked Iran” because of increased oil prices, and that simply stopping those hostilities could free up funding for climate efforts.

“We have lost [the] trust of the international community when it comes to climate,” remarked Rep. Yassamin Ansari (D-Ariz.).

According to recent reports, “I think it is a complete betrayal of our responsibility that Donald Trump has pulled us out of the Paris Agreement not once but twice,” she noted. A Democrat winning the 2028 presidential election would help ensure the US can rejoin that agreement, she added.

It will take time to regain trust in the international community, Ansari noted.

“But we will come back,” she noted, “working 10 times harder, 50 times harder than we did before, to make sure that we are being team players, to make sure that we are… supporting small island developing states and supporting vulnerable African nations.”.

Climate activists reacted cautiously to the promises about the United States’ potential return to the international climate arena.

In a recent development, “We welcome the political shift in the United States that puts the brakes on the reckless dismantling of domestic green policies,” mentioned Harjeet Singh, director of Satat Sampada Climate Foundation. “However, here at COP31 in Antalya, the international community cannot afford to celebrate prematurely or suffer from collective amnesia.”.

Singh said the US has a long history of obstructing climate negotiations across successive administrations and regardless of which party holds power.

In a recent development, “As the world’s largest historical emitter, the US carries an outsized moral and legal responsibility to act,” he mentioned. “Real change will not be measured by who walks through the halls of this summit, but by whether Washington finally ends its expansion of oil, gas, and coal at home and delivers hundreds of billions of dollars in grant-based climate finance to developing countries.”.

Singh remarked until the US pays its fair share to help vulnerable countries recover from climate impacts and transition to sustainable energy systems, “warm words from visiting lawmakers mean very little to communities on the frontlines.”.

Brandon Wu, with ActionAid USA, noted the new Democrat-led House majority must reassert control over the budget and hold the Trump administration accountable for “likely illegal actions like dismantling USAID and gutting foreign assistance” funding approved by Congress.

“What they can deliver to the United Nations process is extremely limited,” he stated, adding that it’s unlikely there will be any sweeping new climate legislation or climate funding in the next two years. What members of Congress can do is lay the groundwork for more ambitious action in a post-Trump era, he added.

While meeting delegates from other countries, Huffman remarked he’s heard both gratitude and optimism, as well as skepticism, about a possible US return to the climate talks.

According to recent reports, “The fact is the US has become kind of an unreliable partner and we’ve lost our credibility,” he said. “So we’ve tried to bring humility to this moment. We’ve got work to do to reclaim our credibility in this institution.”.

It has been revealed that bob Berwyn is an Austria-based reporter who has covered climate science and international climate policy for more than a decade. Previously, he reported on the environment, endangered species, and public lands for several Colorado newspapers, and also worked as editor and assistant editor at community newspapers in the Colorado Rockies.

This story originally appeared on Inside Climate News.

Democrats try to figure out how not to get swept away by the blue wave

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2960 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: The Verge

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • At a conference funded by a billionaire AI investor, a group of centrist Democrats aims to harness the populist moment.﻿.
  • At a conference funded by a billionaire AI investor, a group of centrist Democrats aims to harness the populist moment.﻿.
